title: Macklemore Says His Call to ‘Free Palestine’ Is Not a ‘Criticism’ of Jewish People: ‘None of Us Will Be Free Until We Are All Free’
description: Macklemore is speaking out about his call to “Free Palestine,” which the rapper made while opening for Ed Sheeran on Friday night at New Jersey’s Me
body:
Macklemore is speaking out about his call to “Free Palestine,” which the rapper made while opening for Ed Sheeran on Friday night at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium.

	“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you,” Macklemore said on Saturday night (via Newsweek). “My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.”
	

	He added, “So I say free Palestine, I say free Lebanon, I say free Cuba, I say free Congo, free Sudan, I say free all people in America living in fear of this terrorist organization, ICE. None of us will be free until we are all free.”


	During his Friday night set, Macklemore told the audience that he wanted the people in Gaza and the West Bank to know that he had not forgotten them: “I believe that every human being walking on this earth deserves exactly the same freedom.” The statement caused the Israeli American Council to release a petition that demands that the four-time Grammy winner be removed from the rest of Sheeran’s Loop tour.

	The petition reads, “This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event. The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda.”

schema.headline: Macklemore Says His Call to ‘Free Palestine’ Is Not a ‘Criticism’ of Jewish People: ‘None of Us Will Be Free Until We Are All Free’

title: ‘No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman’ Review: Iraq’s Oscar Submission Offers a Patriotic Anthem to the Kurdish Peshmerga’s Fight Against Islamic State
description: The trope of the lone action hero with near-superhuman strength gets a gender switch in “No Paradise If You Are Killed By A Woman,” a visually impre
body:
The trope of the lone action hero with near-superhuman strength gets a gender switch in “No Paradise If You Are Killed By A Woman,” a visually impressive drama about a resourceful female Peshmerga sniper. Although selected as Iraq’s submission for the Best International Feature Oscar, the third fiction feature from Norwegian-Kurdish helmer Halkawt Mustafa (“Red Heart,” “El Clásico”) may fall between two stools for Western viewers: There’s not enough action for genre fans and the narrative’s blend of melodrama and earnestness may turn off highbrow arthouse viewers. But it’s a different story in MENA territories where Sony/Empire has already nabbed distribution rights. Regional and Kurdish diaspora audiences should appreciate the strong visual and technical craftmanship used in this harrowing tale.
	

	The narrative centers on Vyan (striking London-based Kurdish thesp Avan Jamal, impressive), a 24-year-old Kurdish émigré to Norway who is visiting Iraqi Kurdistan with her parents and younger sister Helin in 2014, when Islamic State (IS) launches an attack. Their parents are murdered and Vyan and Helin are sold as IS sex slaves. Ever resilient, Vyan manages to kill the man who bought her and make her way to Peshmerga territory. There, she joins an elite unit of female fighters as a sniper.


	As Vyan’s poetic voiceover narration states, Peshmerga means “before death” and its fighters enter combat out of strength, not out of fear. Certainly, Vyan is fearless. She reckons that she has killed more than 100 of the enemy in three years. Given that, as the title notes, IS fighters believe that there is “No Paradise If You Are Killed by A Woman,” it’s no wonder they have placed a million-dollar bounty on her head.
	

	After heroically preventing an IS suicide truck bomber in an armored vehicle from attacking her unit’s base, the heavily wounded Vyan returns to Norway to recover. There, a government official (Thorbjørn Harr) offers her a difficult choice: accept a new identity and government protection (they fear the fact that she is an IS target could endanger other Norwegian citizens) or be prosecuted for fighting for another country. Luckily, Norwegian civilians don’t have to worry. A phone call to the family’s old landline confirms that Helin remains trapped in Mosul, in the clutches of an IS fighter known as the Swedish sniper. Loyal Vyan prepares for what may be her final mission: to singlehandedly rescue her sister.

	The last half of the film feels as if it could easily be adapted into a tense video game as it follows Vyan silently creeping through tunnels and crawling through the aftermath of IS carnage. It certainly gives a more detailed picture of how a sniper operates, and the lonely patience required for the job, than Clint Eastwood’s “American Sniper” ever did. Vyan uses logic and the help of friendly Kurdish commander from the Iraqi government forces in Mosul to locate the IS snipers preventing civilians from leaving the devastated city.

	Research for multi-hyphenate Mustafa’s 2015 TV project “The Women ISIS Fears” and his time as a war photographer seeing strong female fighters inspired “No Paradise,” which he dedicates to his daughters. Like the helmer’s previous features, it proudly incorporates Kurdish customs and traditions, from the “singing” that Vyan’s rifle performs to the traditional tunes sung by her Peshmerga captain and the Kurdish commander in Mosul.

	Highlights of a polished technical package include the prowling camerawork of Norwegian DP John Erling H. Fredriksen and the film’s use of actual Mosul locations. The shocking ruins of what was once a thriving population center attest to a brutal military campaign to liberate the ancient city from IS. Also worthy of special mention in a film where the main character spends much of her time in silence is the tension-building sound design by Mattias Eklund and Jan Kasskawo.

schema.headline: ‘No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman’ Review: Iraq’s Oscar Submission Offers a Patriotic Anthem to the Kurdish Peshmerga’s Fight Against Islamic State

title: Elon Musk Documentary Teaser Asks If Billionaire Is the ‘Greatest Living Inventor’ or a ‘Fascist’ Who ‘Has Lost His Mind’
description:
The first teaser trailer for Alex Gibney’s highly anticipated Elon Musk documentary “Musk” has been released.

	The film will world premiere out of
body:
The first teaser trailer for Alex Gibney’s highly anticipated Elon Musk documentary “Musk” has been released.

	The film will world premiere out of competition at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 8 before continuing to the Toronto International Film Festival.

	In the 48-second teaser, montages of spacecrafts and astronautical devices fill the screen while voices giving varied commentary about Musk play in the background. The snippet does not give away much about the plot, but illustrates Musk’s polarizing character. 
	

	“He’s possibly the greatest living inventor. He is the real-life Iron Man. He is one of the greatest builders of all time,” the background voices say. As the montage progresses, the tone of the statements changes. “He is the greatest capitalist in history. He’s chaotic, random, capricious, manifestly cruel and selfish. He’s a fascist,” the backtrack continues. 


	“Elon is a nuke,” the voice in the teaser concludes as a spacecraft hits the ground and implodes, bursting into flames. 

	Gibney first revealed in March 2023 that he had begun work on the documentary and was “many months” into production. Musk responded to news of the project on his X/Twitter account by predicting it would be “a hit piece.” Gibney fired back on the same platform, asking “how would you know?”

	The film, with a nearly four-hour running time, will feature an original song from Talking Heads frontman David Byrne, who wrote and performed the new track entitled “Let Me Sell You a Dream.”

	Gibney directs and produces “Musk,” joined by Jessie Deeter and Erin Edeiken for Jigsaw Productions, Dana O’Keefe for Double Agent, Joey Marra and Zhang Xin for Closer Media and Anonymous Content’s Nick Shumaker and Jessica Grimshaw. Ronan Farrow and Lawrence Wright round out the producing team.

title: ‘Elsinore’ Director Simon Stone, Basking in Telluride’s Glow, on Making a Movie About Love of the Theater, the Peak AIDS Era, and Being ‘100% in the Service of Andrew Scott’
description: The Telluride Film Festival casts a wide net, as almost all festivals of its ilk do, but if it has had any speciality that stands out among many, it
body:
The Telluride Film Festival casts a wide net, as almost all festivals of its ilk do, but if it has had any speciality that stands out among many, it might be the well-earned tearjerker. There is as much crying at Telluride every year as there isn’t in baseball, but with the festival’s emphasis on top-line prestige fare, returning patrons look forward to going through some emotional catharsis in the mountains every Labor Day weekend. Among the 2026 lineup, probably no film got passholders any deeper in their feels than “Elsinore,” starring Andrew Scott and directed by Simon Stone. Their remarkable film dramatizes the true-life story of a well-known British actor — Ian Charleson, of “Chariots of Fire” fame — who died at the peak of the AIDS crisis in 1990, but who spent his last months and weeks staying alive long enough to achieve the life goal of playing Hamlet at the National Theatre.
	

	There won’t be a dry eye in the house when this goes wide, as the cliche goes, but there also won’t be an untickled funny bone, given a performance by Scott that’s almost as drolly funny as it is passionate and heartrending (with no small help from writer Stephen Beresford). And there won’t be any un-warmed hearts among any viewers with a deep love for the life of the theater, since the movie serves as a love letter to stagecraft and community, on top of of most obviously being an ode to the seeming indomitability of Charleson as he bravely forestalled his final bow.


	Stone’s long history as an actor before he became a premier stage director in Australia and then London — before finally moving into film — deeply informs every legit-loving moment of “Elsinore.” Variety spoke with him the day after his new film unspooled in Telluride, where he enjoyed a crowd waiting to give him and Scott yet another ovation in the lobby, some time after the credits rolled. Under his direction, Scott is an instant contender in the best actor face, and Stone may be up for some contending himself.
	

	You told the crowd at the premiere that “Elsinore” was hot off the presses. How recent was it?

	We finished on Wednesday of last week, so it’s a week and a half old. It’s very fresh. I think we were very lucky. Focus happened to have a slot that was unoccupied in their fall slate. And I think of course they recognized what Andrew’s doing in the movie is kind of undeniable (for awards consideration), and also that it’s a film that really resonates with audiences. I think that when you’re dealing with studios who still believe in watching movies in the theater, a film like this is like catnip. It’s specially made as an advocate for the theater-going experience. And I think all that catapulted us into a schedule that meant that we had to go fast, because we had to get to here (Telluride). We’re releasing in November, and when we release the movie, it will have been about 10 months from when we shot it. That’s lightning.

	I’m not sure of comparable stories about how quickly a film turns around, and that is a testament to the work of everyone who told that story, and how prepared Andrew was. I guess we were all. I’d directed “Hamlet” on stage; Andrew had played Hamlet on stage; I had directed at the National Theatre. We knew all of these environments and this community. When you live that life for a long time, you want to be true to it, so there was an insistence on veracity and honesty that held true.



	

					‘Elsinore’ director Simon Stone at the Telluride Film Festival
									Chris Willman/Variety
	



	We all probably could have guessed that Andrew had done “Hamlet” on stage.

	He had to relearn all the soliloquies, and I dadidn’t know exactly what scenes what bits were from, so I had to remind myself. But I essentially directed that production of “Hamlet” live, and we shot a documentary of me directing it, essentially, but I had an avatar of Johnny Flynn pretending to be me. But nobody knew when they walked into that rehearsal room on those days how it was gonna be staged. I staged it live, the way you would in a rehearsal room. What you’re watching in all of those rehearsal sequences is Andrew genuinely improvising. I mean, he knew his lines, but the idea of how he does it and where he does it, how it… That thing where Johnny (as the director) goes, “Don’t be afraid of intimacy. Hold each other,” those are all lines that I, a minute before we rolled, had fed into Johnny’s ear. Because I direct plays all the time, so I was like, “Well, this is the easiest way of us shooting this — for me to just direct this play.”
	

	What were the other actors in the “Hamlet” scenes told about the story or about what to do?

	They knew the backstory because in London, Ian’s story is one of those myths that is really meaningful, and a lot of his friends were in the film. And it’s a love letter to what theater is — it’s right there. They all wanted to do that, and to make it genuine, as opposed to like… You see so many depictions of theater as this over-the-top, self-centered, performative thing, and I wanted to show it as a crucible, as a shelter, as a safe place.



	

					Andrew Scott stars as Ian Charleson, who was dying of AIDS while playing Hamlet, in ELSINORE.Credit: Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC
									Anthony Dickenson
	



	There is a scene when Ian starts coming clean about his illness with the rest of the “Hamlet” cast, and a viewer might wonder if, in a scene like that, there will be one token person who seems uncomfortable after learning he has AIDS, but they appear uniformly supportive. It does show what theater buffs hope the inner theater community is really like.

	That’s right. I also think the theater community is a group of outsiders. It’s a bunch of freaks and geeks, and the reason we got into it was to share a common humanity, despite not being an average human being. There are a lot of parallels with the gay community at that time, and there is a distinct overlap, obviously. There are a lot of gay kids that ended up in theater because it was a place to express things that they felt that they couldn’t express elsewhere. So I think it’s a kind of rallying cry for acceptance and truth. And when we screened it last night, so many people were so heartfelt in really trying to express how moved they were by having felt seen or having felt someone in their life was seen by this film. That’s worth a million reviews or a million articles. It’s just a single person saying “That meant so much to me,” and I think Ian would feel really happy that that’s his legacy.

	You must know what you’ve got on your hands. Did you expect the kind of reaction you’ve gotten in Telluride?

	I would never have the hubris to assume that my reaction to something is gonna be someone else’s reaction to something. But I do know that I’ve made it in the spirit of heartfelt positivity about the joy we can find in life in the face of adversity. I think we’re living in a time in history where things feel so insecure geopolitically, socially — so divisive, so much difference. We’re focused on difference all the time in the media or in politics, like what separates us. I knew that people would really appreciate a film which is about no matter how different we are, we have to be together, otherwise all is lost…. The final scene seems like a triumph of an individual, but it’s not. It’s a group of people saying, “You are one of us.” The final scene is a flashback, because by the time you see the final scene, he’s already passed. So what you know is that you’re being let into what might have been his last memory as he disappeared, and it’s a memory of being with a group of people who said “We love you.”
	

	Where do you think we’re at now in terms of people doing stories about “the AIDS era”? In terms of major films, it’s receded a bit.

	Well, like all of these things, I think they need to recede. You know, thank God people aren’t making so many World War II movies. Every second movie in the ’50s was about the Second World War, and it had to be, because it was the big reckoning. When I was growing up, most multiplexes had one Second World War film in it at any point. And if you chart the history of Hollywood, you realize that becomes less and less and less and less. And, and there, of course, is the danger because at the end of the day, it was an important kind of reckoning, and it was an important catharsis. Then, of course, people go, “Well, that can’t be the only thing we’re focusing on,” because at a certain point it becomes fetishistic. I do think that that’s the same thing with any cataclysmic event: It needs a real analysis, but then it also needs the catharsis, which is we’ve explored — what it was about us that we got wrong. In the AIDS epidemic, it was very much a marginalization of a group of people that we thought that that was their problem rather than ours. I hope that we have learnt the lesson from that.

	I also think that it’s because unless you’re in certain parts of the Third World, you’re not dealing with the idea of fatality if you get an HIV diagnosis. So all of these things mean that it kind of becomes less immediately relevant or immediately urgent. But that doesn’t mean that it doesn’t represent all sorts of lessons that we can learn about ourselves now. And I think that what’s great about this film is that AIDS is a context in the film. It’s a situation. In the same way that Martin’s film (Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” also showing in Telluride) is (set) in the ’70s…. The idea of American intervention in overseas political environments, that’s a context. But at the same time, (“Wild Horse Nine”) is a conversation about what happens when arrogant white men think that they can tell other people how to live, and that then suddenly feels relevant to now.

	And I think that we found an equivalent thing with this. AIDS is a context, but it’s a conversation about divisiveness in communities, about the endless attempts to separate ourselves from each other and to create taboos in minority communities about what’s acceptable and what’s not acceptable. And I think that this film is is about: stop looking for everything that’s different about you and find something that’s similar. Find the common ground. Ian did that so beautifully in his life.
	

	So I think it’s a very long-winded answer to your question about the relevance of the AIDS movie. But I think that the great triumph is that when “Philadelphia” was made, it had to be the only topic of that film, and we’ve got to a point where it’s one of five strands. And that’s an achievement. That’s a triumph.

	Dealing with a terminal illness is closer to universal than not. People die unexpectedly, of course, too, but for the most part…

	Yeah facing the end of life is a pretty common thing. The beauty of what he does in the movie is that he looks into the abyss and he finds hope. And weirdly, I was talking to some people where it was like, “Last night I was crying my eyes out, but today I feel really good.” I was like, that’s a common response to people who watch the film, because it’s true catharsis. It’s like a good session with your therapist. It’s like, yeah, it was painful to witness for a second, but at the end of the day, what it gave you was hope, and that’s a great thing to have. Because he faced the end willingly and with beauty, and that grace is extraordinary.

	You said it was Andrew’s performance that put Focus into a hurry in wanting to get this out at a premium time this fall. What does his work on this mean to you, as his director?

	Well, I mean, Andrew is one of those actors that I think we took for granted for a long time, thinking that he’ll always turn up and he’ll always be amazing. And I think this is one of the first projects where we had to be as amazing as he was — that he wasn’t just in the service of what we were doing. I think we as an industry have done that a lot. We’ve hired him to be in the service of what we need to do, and he’s always turned up, he’s delivered, he’s been brilliant. But this is the first one that’s been really 100% about what can we do to be in the service of you, Andrew, and he deserves the movie in the same way that Ian deserves this portrait of him. And I feel so honored to have kind of been a priest of that temple.

schema.headline: ‘Elsinore’ Director Simon Stone, Basking in Telluride’s Glow, on Making a Movie About Love of the Theater, the Peak AIDS Era, and Being ‘100% in the Service of Andrew Scott’

title: ‘Look Back’ Review: Once Past the Over- Preciousness of a Child’s World, Hirokazu Kore-eda’s Manga Adaptation Becomes a Moving Tribute to Friendship
description: There’s barely an adult in sight in Hirokazu Kore-eda’s “Look Back,” where anyone out of school age is marginalized practically to the point of supe
body:
There’s barely an adult in sight in Hirokazu Kore-eda’s “Look Back,” where anyone out of school age is marginalized practically to the point of superfluidity. Like much in the first half of this sweet — at times too sweet — adaptation from Tatsuki Fujimoto’s manga of the same title, also made into an animated film in 2024, the preciousness of a child’s world can create a barrier for those who don’t automatically melt at the sight of a youngster’s smile. But then, as often happens in Kore-eda’s child-focused body of work, there’s a moment when, unexpectedly, what’s on screen suddenly hits a point of transcendence and resistance falls away. That moment can take a bit of time to come, but the payoff is worth the wait.
	

	Fujino (Furi Nanase) is the undisputed star of fourth grade, encouraged by her teacher Mr. Tamai (Kankuro Kudo) and exalted by her peers for the manga strips she draws and shares at school. She thrives on being the queen, so when impressively advanced manga strips appear in school drawn by Kyomoto (Rokka Okada), a reclusive classmate no one has seen, Fujino is not pleased. In response, she redoubles her efforts, neglecting her friends and family in order to once again be the best.


	Two years later it’s elementary school graduation time and Mr. Tamai asks Fujino to deliver Kyomoto’s diploma to her home. Though not thrilled with the assignment, she enters the girl’s home, down a corridor piled high with notebooks, looks at the “do not enter” sign and turns away, but not before one of her manga strips gets blown under the door. Just when Fujino leaves, out runs Kyomoto in a tizzy — because she recognizes the girl as the creator of the school’s beloved manga strips, a true master, or “sensei.” This adulation is all Fujino needs to take Kyomoto under her wing, and soon the two are inseparable, collaborating on strips where Fujino writes the stories and draws the figures while Kyomoto does the backgrounds.
	

	Clearly more advanced than the average schoolgirls, the two enter a competition sponsored by the Shueisha publishing house, whose editor (Masaki Suda) recognizes their talents and publishes their first story. Success comes rapidly to the teens, now played by Natsuki Deguchi (Fujino) and Aju Makita (Kyomoto), but their roles remain the same, which suits Fujino just fine. When high school ends the Shueisha editor offers them a series, but Kyomoto wants to go to art school instead. Fujino sees it as a betrayal and determines to be a manga star with or without Kyomoto’s help.

	For all of Fujino’s rather full-on sunniness, the truth is she’s a prima donna who lashes out if she doesn’t get her own way. What happens next at first feels like a dreadful narrative misstep, seemingly reinforcing the idea that cutting oneself off from others can save them from life’s travails. Those already familiar with the original manga know better, but so should audiences acquainted with Kore-eda’s humanistic approach to characters: who we are and how we experience the world together, rather than our achievements, is our real saving grace.

	As long as audiences accept that this is basically a two-hander, the absence of any other characters with more than stick-figure attributes becomes less problematic. Fujino’s mother exists solely to feed her family and clean house, while Kyomoto’s mother is barely glimpsed — at times it’s difficult to be sure whether the withdrawn girl is real or just a figment of Fujino’s imagination, since for some time that’s the only place she seems to legitimately inhabit.

	Sound design is a key element of this world, from the sounds of graphite on paper acting like a musical accompaniment in tandem with Yuta Bandoh’s pleasant score, to the more mechanically produced noise of digital pencils on computer screens. The director’s partiality for seasonal changes is on full display, from brightly colored, sun-tinged summers to autumnal glows and winter’s snowy pleasures. Each season is given major prominence in the children’s world, though why Kore-eda chose a generally pale palette of diffused light isn’t clear. Unless, that is, it’s designed as a contrast to the later saturations of the girls’ more elaborate designs, and the manga animation insert that stirringly helps to bring things to a bittersweet, though deeply satisfying, close.

schema.headline: ‘Look Back’ Review: Once Past the Over- Preciousness of a Child’s World, Hirokazu Kore-eda’s Manga Adaptation Becomes a Moving Tribute to Friendship

title: MPA Signs Two Lumiere Summit Declarations, Joins Roundtables With Presidents Macron and Lee
description: The Motion Picture Association signed two declarations at the Lumière Summit on Monday, adding its name alongside those of governments and private s
body:
The Motion Picture Association signed two declarations at the Lumière Summit on Monday, adding its name alongside those of governments and private sector organizations worldwide to the Lumière Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image and the Declaration on Strengthened International Cooperation in the Fight Against Film and Audiovisual Piracy. 

	The summit was co-chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.
	

	MPA chair and CEO Charles Rivkin participated in two separate business roundtables – one with President Lee focused on the industry’s engagement with Korea’s creative sector, and one with President Macron on the future of the industry and opportunities to strengthen ties with France’s creative sector. Both sessions included MPA member studio CEOs.


	“Our industry is fueled by a simple proposition: audiences love great stories, well told. … From the U.S. to France to Korea and beyond, we each have a stake in ensuring that our industry remains a force for openness, a source of investment, and a driver of jobs, growth, and opportunity. This summit proved a vital forum to translate that common ground into greater cooperation,” Rivkin said.

	Emilie Anthonis, president and managing director of the MPA’s Europe, Middle East and Africa region, took part in a session on Korea’s expanding role in the worldwide film and television industry, which also featured President Lee. She also appeared in a session titled “The Race Against Piracy: A Global Challenge,” where she highlighted the work of the MPA and the Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE) – the world’s leading anti-piracy coalition – in addressing the cross-border scale of content theft. Anthonis welcomed the summit’s recognition that protecting intellectual property and fighting piracy are fundamental to sustaining the creative economy.
	

	The MPA’s member studios are Netflix, Paramount Pictures, Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, Sony Pictures, Universal Studios, The Walt Disney Studios and Warner Bros. Discovery.

schema.headline: MPA Signs Two Lumiere Summit Declarations, Joins Roundtables With Presidents Macron and Lee

title: ‘The Spiral’ Review: Paolo Strippoli’s Lurid Faustian Tragedy Shores Up His Reputation as Italy’s New Horror Virtuoso
description: We don’t get a close enough look to see if the Devil actually wears Prada, but regardless, in Paolo Strippoli‘s new horror romp “The Spiral,” she’s
body:
We don’t get a close enough look to see if the Devil actually wears Prada, but regardless, in Paolo Strippoli‘s new horror romp “The Spiral,” she’s very chicly turned out indeed: Cool, crisp and collected in a tightly belted camel trenchcoat, hair pristinely bobbed and lips perfectly rouged, wielding a cigarette like a laser pointer. As played with her signature husky-flutey delivery by Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, this film’s Lucifer has seemingly stepped straight out of a film noir, though she hardly needs to use her femme fatale wiles to seduce well-to-do fashionista and mother-of-two Anna (Jasmine Trinca) — she just needs to prey, with casual malice, on any parent’s worst fears regarding their families, and if that also means asking Anna to choose between her children, so much the better. Step on our necks, mother Mephistopheles, and let the kids suffer the consequences.
	

	A faintly absurd Faustian fable blown up to grand guignol proportions through Strippoli’s brash formal command of his favorite genre, “The Spiral” doesn’t add up to an awful lot, but the sum of its parts is flashily entertaining enough. It’s the fourth feature from the 33-year-old Italian horror specialist, and his first to be programmed in the main competition at Venice — a status upgrade that, given the new film’s lurid but quite superficial pleasures, might strike some as premature. 


	In fact, it might be a year late. “The Spiral” arrives hot on the heels of Strippoli’s third feature “The Holy Boy,” a wickedly clever, creepy tale of small-town trauma, terror and faith that was a standout of Venice’s out-of-competition sidebar a year ago, and is an altogether more layered, probing and frankly frightening film than this one. Perhaps this year’s selection is the festival’s mea culpa; perhaps the star presence of veteran Euro-arthouse queen Bruni Tedeschi makes all the difference. Either way, this stylish hokum secures Strippoli’s claim to horror-auteur status, and should see him cross over into the international elevated-genre market. It would be no great surprise if Hollywood remake rights are negotiated before the film even makes it to U.S. screens, while major studios looking to zhuzh up their upcoming horror properties could do far worse than to take Strippoli’s card.
	

	It certainly begins as it intends to continue, going straight in with the ear-splitting attack of Quentin Collette’s maximalist sound design — all manner of natural and unnatural phenomena shrieking in unison as the camera opens on a hand clutching a plane armrest for dear life, as extreme turbulence batters the aircraft hither and thither. Outside the window, a none-too-encouraging cyclone is forming in the clouds: the first of several spirals in the film’s image system, which, like many passing details in “The Spiral,” look cool and unnerving without leading anywhere in particular. 

	Cut to terra ferma, where the almighty rainstorm soaking the streets of Rome seems a comparatively trifling bit of weather. Anna, damp and frazzled, turns up unannounced at the door of her apprehensive adult daughter Alice (Romana Maggiora Vergano), insisting she has a terrible family secret to reveal, that can’t wait a minute longer. Her timing isn’t great; as it turns out, it never has been. 

	We rewind a quarter-century or so to the first of the film’s formally marked chapters, each titled after a different member of the family in question, though the story’s point of view doesn’t notably shift between them. In sunny Bari, Anna and husband Walter (Adriano Giannini) head up a picture-perfect model family — so very model, in fact, that seven-year-old Alice (Gabriella Telegrafo) has just been cast in a Barilla pasta ad. That goes out the window when, at a lush garden party on their luxury estate, Alice is brutally and unaccountably mauled by their bull terrier; ER doctors save her life, but as they bluntly inform her parents, they’re unlikely to save her leg.

	With the threat of amputation looming, Anna heads to the church chapel — an ominous space merging gaudy Italo-modernism with aggressively Catholic candlelight, one of several coups here by production designer Marcello Di Carlo — to breathe, cry and pray. God doesn’t answer, but someone else does. Enter Bruni Tedeschi’s unnamed eavesdropper (“The Stranger,” to translate the film’s original Italian title), who at first gently commiserates with the distraught mother, before revealing some unsettling knowledge of the family’s situation, and proposing an even more unsettling solution: She can ensure that little Alice keeps her leg, but at some physical cost to her older brother Tobia (Alessandro Carbonara). Scarcely believing this outlandish offer and not in her right mind to begin with, Anna agrees.
	

	Cue years of staggered, steadily worsening consequences, unboxed by Strippoli with gruesome relish. It’s for viewers to decide whether the streak of ableism and body-shaming that accompanies this fallout is the film’s failing or the work of the Devil herself, in what arguably amounts to a sick joke about Italian image-consciousness, Catholic guilt, or perhaps nothing all that deep. Mostly, Strippoli wants us to enjoy the loud, bumpy ride, and to a point, we do. 

	But his script winds up spiraling inwards rather than outwards. The belabored flashback structure saps some tension from the enterprise, while Anna’s dreadful secret (revealed rather early in proceedings) doesn’t really build in physical, moral or spiritual resonance, leaving it to Strippoli’s enjoyably vulgar, pedal-to-the-metal aesthetic to gee up the film’s narrative sputtering engine. He does, however, give Bruni Tedeschi’s very soigné Satan a few more opportunities to re-up the terms and conditions of her initial dastardly contract, giving the proceedings a welcome injection of camp energy each time. We all knew the Devil has all the best tunes — who knew she has all the best shoes too?

title: ‘Alpha Gang’ Review: Cate Blanchett, Chris Pine and an All-Star Cast Play Space Aliens in David and Nathan Zellner’s Endearingly Goofy Sci-Fi Spoof
description:
Sep 7, 2026 10:36am PT	
	

	
		‘Alpha Gang’ Review: Cate Blanchett, Chris Pine and an All-Star Cast Play Space Aliens in David and N
body:
Sep 7, 2026 10:36am PT	
	

	
		‘Alpha Gang’ Review: Cate Blanchett, Chris Pine and an All-Star Cast Play Space Aliens in David and Nathan Zellner’s Endearingly Goofy Sci-Fi Spoof
	

	With a ‘50s biker gang aesthetic and a premise that loosely recalls 'Pleasantville,' the fiercely indie brothers’ latest oddity is a mostly winsome ensemble affair where everyone commits to the bit.
	
			


			
			
	

									TIFF
	

		
	
				
				
	Among the greatest cinematic mysteries of our time, when it’s harder than ever to make movies, is the fact that David and NathanZellner continue to realize their uncompromisingly DIY, endearingly childlike vision through an indie filmography that only seems to grow in scale and purpose. It’s a welcome miracle that the duo who once captured the rhythms of childhood in their own idiosyncratic way (“Kid-Thing”), channeled compassion for those who might think the buried “Fargo” treasure is real (“Kumiko the Treasure Hunter”), and made a goofily unhinged groom out of Robert Pattinson nearly a decade before “The Drama” got there (“Damsel”), continue to play in their lovable sandbox.
	

	For most audiences, the Zellners’ rhythms and textures are an acquired taste of sorts, like oysters or Marmite, that some would swear by, and others couldn’t fathom. Thankfully, many of the finest actors out there seem to revere them. In fact, quite a few of them — including Léa Seydoux, Cate Blanchett (also a producer), Chris Pine and Kelvin Harrison Jr. — turn up and gleefully let loose in the brothers’ latest indie oddity “Alpha Gang,” about a group of isolated, leather-clad space aliens aiming to conquer the earth while donned in ‘50s biker gear. Because, well, why not?


	The story’s time period is purposely indistinct: We might be somewhere in the mid-20th century if the gang’s romantically fitted greaser outfits, meticulously sculpted hairdos, and disarming doo-wop musical tastes — played out of an old-timey jukebox — are any indication. Then again, who knows where and when any of this is happening, given that many earthlings also turn up throughout “Alpha Gang.” They represent figures of various real-world wars throughout history, tasked to eradicate the blue-blooded aliens: sometimes in tanks, with bazookas and hand grenades, sometimes in carriages and with vintage weapons. Still with me?
	

	Trying to kill them first are the group of Alphas One to Six, played by Seydoux and Harrison Jr., as well as Doona Bae, Riley Keough, Dave Bautista and Lily-Rose Depp. Most of the time, they keep a straight, frozen face while dancing to ‘50s love songs with robotic moves. And they are all alarmed about this fast-spreading human disease called emotions. What if they catch it and regretfully display joy, sadness, anger and so on, slowly losing their powers? Late to the party, Keough’s Alpha Six, who appears on earth in a playful scene out of a vintage sci-fi, gets warned about these dangerous things called feelings by Seydoux’s Alpha One. But Six has bigger things to worry about, like the explosive diarrhea attack all Alphas have to endure when they enter Earth.

	Yes, there are toilet jokes throughout “Alpha Gang,” and the funniest one is a running gag about the mystery Alpha who consistently leaves the seat up and pees all over it. Still, the most appealing quality of this film — directed jointly by the Zellners, but written by David only — is how much undeniable fun the cast seems to having delivering truly ridiculous lines with a straight face, like when a love-hungry Alpha Three (Harrison Jr.) asks a little bird to go steady with him. 

	He isn’t the only one losing himself in feelings. Alphas Two (Bautista), Four (Depp) and Five (Bae) also secretly harbor awakenings, with One and Six projecting anger and frustration in excess. While this construct, where emotions soften the aliens’ stiff edges, especially recalls Gary Ross’ “Pleasantville,” the already colorful Alphas don’t turn even more Technicolor. Instead, they tear up, they fear each other and they get blue periods. Again, why not?

	A turning point arrives with Chris Pine’s entry as the latest Alpha, who is consistently the film’s funniest presence as soon as he joins it. The whole cast commits to the bit, having undoubtedly shown up to play— still, there is something about Pine’s overdone mannerisms that land with the most uproarious laughter. When a rival, ‘80s-style gang called Beta shows up with an eye-patched and hilarious Cate Blanchett in their ranks (wait until you hear her accent), the mayhem only escalates from there. It’s evident that the Zellners have conceived the Alphas and Betas with a “Terminator”-like logic: Betas are the more advanced aliens, refusing to join forces with the relatively naïve Alphas.
	

	There will be body parts severed, much (blue) blood spilled, and extreme violence erupting in every corner of the Zellners’ brutalist designs and impressively immersive world-building that needs to be seen to be believed. And viewers’ mileage will certainly vary with this peculiar, fun little concoction on seclusion, connection and the need to belong that can’t hide its undercurrent of melancholy about the sorry state of a divided world. Shortly after it begins to overstay its welcome, yielding diminishing returns, the film thankfully concludes — reminding us that cinema can afford to make more room for uncompromising visions and kooky little artworks with something to say and some fun to spare.

title: Summer Box Office Breaks All-Time Record With $4.67 Billion
description: Need proof the movies are really, truly back? The summer box office was already the biggest since COVID upended the industry in 2020 — and now the s
body:
Need proof the movies are really, truly back? The summer box office was already the biggest since COVID upended the industry in 2020 — and now the season has become the highest-grossing of all time. Domestic ticket sales from May 1 through Labor Day on Sept. 7 stand at $4.76 billion, according to Rentrak. Revenues surpassed the long-held record set in 2013 with $4.755 billion, anchored by “Iron Man 3,” “Despicable Me 2” and “Man of Steel.”
	

	This summer’s benchmark comes with two major caveats: Ticket sales from more than a decade ago weren’t adjusted for inflation, and popcorn season was slightly longer (running at 130 days compared to 123 days in 2013) because of Labor Day’s placement on the calendar. Still, it’s a significant milestone because it signals that after five years of uncertainty about the movie business, people have fallen back in love with the silver screen.


	While the summer box office record marks an important turning point for movie theaters, the numbers are only part of the story,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “What makes this summer uniquely important and potentially pivotal is that, for many people, it may have been the season that reminded them just how much fun it is to go to the movies. That can inspire future moviegoing, create a new generation of theatergoers and, with so many great films still ahead, keep that momentum going.”


	This summer is also notable as the first in history where each of the four months generated above $1 billion, with May bringing in $1.07 billion, June powering to $1.08 billion, July earning $1.18 billion and August soaring to $1.27 billion, according to Rentrak. Popcorn season, which runs from early May through Labor Day, is crucial because revenues for those months represent 40% of the annual box office. This summer is only the second since the pandemic in which ticket sales surpassed $4 billion. The first time was in 2023, when “Barbenheimer” fever buoyed grosses to $4.09 billion. In 2019, the last “normal” period at the box office, summer revenues climbed to $4.3 billion, thanks to “Avengers: Endgame” and several other billion-dollar blockbusters. In 2018, popcorn season reached $4.42 billion with “Avengers: Infinity War” and “Incredibles 2” among the highest-grossing movies.
	

	This season, studios succeeded with time-tested franchise sequels like “Toy Story 5” and “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” as well as Gen Z-fueled sleeper hits like “Obsession” and “Backrooms.” Much of the credit for the potential milestone belongs to Sony’s Marvel adventure “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which has been a behemoth with $923 million domestically and $2.4 billion globally to date. Universal’s Christopher Nolan epic “The Odyssey” also shattered expectations with $589 million in North America and $1.62 billion worldwide. Those triumphs helped offset some major bombs, including Disney’s live-action “Moana,” Warner Bros. and DC’s “Supergirl” and Amazon MGM’s “Masters of the Universe.”

	Over Labor Day weekend, Sony’s Marvel juggernaut “Spider-Man: Brand New Home” was No. 1 for the sixth consecutive frame with $23.5 million during the four-day holiday frame. With unprecedented staying power, “Brand New Day” will soon surpass 2015’s “Star Wars: The Force Awakens” ($936 million, not adjusted for inflation) as the highest-grossing movie of all time at the domestic box office. Meanwhile, it’s already the third-biggest release ever globally behind 2009’s “Avatar” ($2.9 billion) and “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.7 billion). 

	“The Odyssey” secured second place with $17.3 million over the holiday after eight weekends on the big screen. Imax has contributed $486 million globally, representing a massive 30% of the film’s total box office tally. 

	Third place went to another holdover, “Coyote vs. Acme,” with $15.8 million from 3,727 venues over the four days. With great reviews and positive audience scores, “Looney Tunes” spinoff has been a hit with $38.3 million domestically after two weekends of release. It was originally set at Warner Bros. before the studio shelved the completed film as a $30 million tax write-off. That prompted outrage from the creative community, leading Warner Bros. to allow the filmmaking team to shop “Coyote vs. Acme” around town before selling it to indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment.

	Newcomer “By Any Means,” an R-rated thriller from Paramount, stumbled at No. 4 with 9.3 million from 2,903 theaters from Friday to Monday. Directed by Elegance Bratton, “By Any Means” centers around the unlikely partnership between a young Black FBI agent (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) and a notorious mafia hitman (Mark Wahlberg) as they investigate a wave of brutal killings targeting civil rights leaders. It carries a $30 million production budget, funded by Hammerstone Studios.
	

	Two other new holiday releases, Lionsgate’s anxiety-inducing sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” and A24’s action thriller “Onslaught,” failed to even crack the top 10.

	“Fall 2: Deadpoint” crash-landed at No. 12 with $2.8 million at 1,704 venues over the holiday weekend. Those ticket sales are similar to its predecessor, 2022’s survival thriller “Fall,” which opened to $2.5 million. That film managed to climb to $7.2 million domestically and $18 million globally by the end of its run, becoming a modest success against a mere $3 million budget. The sequel follows two friends who travel to Thailand and get trapped at 4,000 feet after a sudden rockslide.

	“Onslaught” fared even worse, debuting in 13th place with $2.2 million from 1,918 theaters through its first four days. Directed by Adam Wingard (“Godzilla vs. Kong”), “Onslaught” stars Adria Arjona as an army sniper who struggles to protect her young daughter from an army of genetically engineered super soldiers.

title: Luca Guadagnino on Casting Hollywood A-Listers in Subversive Roles: ‘I Have Worked With Some of the Finest’
description: Luca Guadagnino discussed his warm rapport with Hollywood movie stars on Monday at the Venice Film Festival, one year after being on the Lido with h
body:
Luca Guadagnino discussed his warm rapport with Hollywood movie stars on Monday at the Venice Film Festival, one year after being on the Lido with his Julia Roberts-starrer “After the Hunt.”

	During a wide-ranging master class the Italian director, who was born in Palermo, Sicily, to an Algerian mother and a Sicilian father – and whose career trajectory has been a long road full of twists and turns that have taken him to Hollywood – was asked about whether he likes casting top stars, such as Roberts, Daniel Craig, Tilda Swinton and Ralph Fiennes, in films that tend to subvert their conventional image with global audiences, as is the case with “Bond” star Craig in “Queer.”
	

	“The truth, the banal truth, is that I am enamored with actors and definitely in love with my actors,” Guadagnino said. “So it’s a very tender emotion for me to work with them. We are like children playing on the beach, kind of creating these sandcastles. Finding ways to express what we want to express, and trying in a way to be truthful and not banal,” he explained.


	“I’ve been lucky because, honestly, I have worked with some of the finest, most committed, bold performers I could have worked with. But I think they know that I love them,” Guadagnino added.

	The feeling tends to be mutual.

	That was clear when Julia Roberts arrived last year at the Venice Film Festival to promote “After the Hunt” wearing a cardigan emblazoned with Guadagnino’s face.

	“Julia is fantastic,” Guadagnino told the packed room. “Every day of that shoot with her was quite inspiring.” Throughout the process of prepping and shooting “After The Hunt,” Roberts was knitting, he recounted. “And when I celebrated my birthday on the shoot of the movie, on Aug. 10 of that year, not only did Julia throw a party for me, but she gave me this present: It was the scarf she was knitting. It’s one of the most precious presents I have.”
	

	Guadagnino kicked off his career thanks to his ability to charm movie stars.

	In 1999, he made “The Protagonists,” a faux experimental doc in which Tilda Swinton and some pals try to reconstruct the motiveless murder of a London waiter. Guadagnino had become obsessed with Swinton after seeing her in Derek Jarman’s “Caravaggio” and cornered her at a Jarman retrospective in Rome, striking up a friendship that blossomed into a creative partnership.

	Swinton eventually went on to play a restrained society dame who gradually bursts out of her loveless Milanese marriage in 2009’s “I Am Love.” “The idea of ‘I Am Love’ started with this image of a woman in a big, big mansion and feeling her feeling of displacement and loneliness,” Guadagnino said, adding: “I understand very well what it means to be estranged and strangled by being in a place where you don’t belong or you thought you belonged and you don’t. And in a way, it is fatal.”

	One place where Guadagnino definitely doesn’t belong is swimming pools.

	“I cannot swim,” he said, discussing “A Bigger Splash,” his 2015 sunshine, sex, food and rock-n-roll-filled remake of French thriller “La piscine,” starring Swinton and Ralph Fiennes.

	“If you put me in the water where I can’t touch the ground, I will drown. So I’m quite terrified by water, by the sea. Totally terrified. And by pools, for sure,” he added.

	In 2017, “Call Me By Your Name” bowed from Sundance, making a splash that reverberated with Italian critics and audiences after it scored Oscar nominations for best picture, actor – Timothée Chalamet’s role as Elio in the film launched his career – adapted screenplay and song. Guadagnino revealed that some of the shades of blue etched into that film “were just a big, big mistake made by the [processing] lab.”

	“I have never been able to reshoot anything in my life because A: I’m very practical. And B: I never had the means to do that. So, I watched this thing, and I said: ‘This is miraculous, because those flashes of light, to me, are the butterflies in Elio’s stomach. And so we kept them in the movie.'”

	Tomorrow Venice will unveil Guadagnino’s sprawling seven-hour Bernardo Bertolucci documentary “Joie de Vivre” in two parts, the first screening on Sept. 8, and the second on Sept. 9. Guadagnino will receive the festival’s Cartier Glory to the Filmmaker Award ahead of the first screening.

title: 'South Park' Mocks Donald Trump After Winning Emmy
description:
'South Park' to Trump
                          Here's the Emmy You Never Won!!!
body:
'South Park' to Trump
                          Here's the Emmy You Never Won!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 7, 2026
                            3:15 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "South Park" just added another Emmy to its trophy case ... and immediately handed President Trump the punchline.
      
    
            The Comedy Central series won Outstanding Animated Program Sunday for "Sermon On The 'Mount," an episode that heavily satirized Trump and even depicted him in bed with Satan.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            After the win, the show's social media account posted an image of its animated Trump clutching the trophy with the message, "You finally got your Emmy."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The joke goes back to Trump's history with the awards -- "The Apprentice" scored Emmy nominations in 2004 and 2005 but never took home the trophy, something Trump has publicly complained about over the years.
      
    
            Sunday's victory marked "South Park's" fifth Emmy in the animated program category.
      
    
            So, after decades of waiting, Trump finally got an Emmy ... he just had to move to South Park to get it.

title: Armed Man Arrested After Scary Confrontation With Ohio Gov. Candidate Amy Acton
description:
Gov. Candidate Amy Acton
                          Targeted by Armed Man at Ohio Fair
body:
Gov. Candidate Amy Acton
                          Targeted by Armed Man at Ohio Fair
                          Suspect in Custody
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 7, 2026
                            8:18 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton was the target of a frightening confrontation Sunday when an armed man allegedly forced his way through a crowd toward her at the Canfield Fair.
      
    
            Acton was speaking at a Mahoning County Democratic Party tent when 38-year-old Patrick Havas allegedly barreled through attendees ... knocking several people to the ground as he moved toward the candidate.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Authorities say Havas was carrying a Taser, brass knuckles, and two pistols ... although none of the weapons were drawn, the Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office added.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Acton was not hurt, but multiple people were injured in the chaos. Witnesses described an elderly man and woman being knocked down as Havas pushed through the crowd.
      
    
            Law enforcement quickly intervened and arrested Havas. He's been booked for disorderly conduct and 2 counts of assault.
      
    
            Acton's campaign praised the rapid response from authorities and condemned political violence.
      
    
            The incident has drawn bipartisan outrage, with Republican Gov. Mike DeWine and Acton's GOP opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, both denouncing what happened.
      
    
            Acton later returned to campaigning, appearing at a Labor Day event and telling supporters the incident underscored why she is running for governor.
